title: Emerging Markets’ Second Balance Sheet
text:
Emerging Markets’ Second Balance Sheet

Rohan Daswani

Gavekal Research | 13 Oct 2026

Sovereign wealth funds are turning their financial firepower toward domestic investment, reflecting a shift in how governments manage national savings and pursue development. In countries engaged in strategic competition with the US, the trend is partly driven by a desire for greater financial autonomy. In the Persian Gulf, it also reflects fiscal pressures arising from lost oil production and the need to repair infrastructure damaged by the US-led conflict with Iran and its proxies. But even before the latest war in the Middle East began, SWFs were changing where they invested their capital and how they financed their activities.Whatever their political orientation and governance arrangements, many sovereign wealth funds have evolved from defensive repositories of savings into more aggressive development agencies and instruments of international influence. Increasingly, they are not simply recycling accumulated surpluses into overseas assets, but borrowing to expand their balance sheets and finance investment at home. This shift promises to accelerate domestic growth, but also brings greater financial risks.
